dateConvention: Arabic chroniclers dated events by the Islamic (Hijri) lunar calendar; every date here is the standard Julian equivalent given in modern references (all before 1582). After 945 the caliphs kept their title while Buyid amirs and then Seljuk sultans held real power; grouped cards cover those stretches, and the caliphs remained Abbasids throughout.
epilogue: In 1261 the Mamluks set up a surviving Abbasid as caliph in Cairo. His line reigned there as figureheads until the Ottoman conquest of 1517; the Ottomans then claimed the title until 1924.

reigns.tagline: The man who toppled a dynasty in one battle
reigns.cameToPower: Hailed at Kufa, then won at the Zab
reigns.previously: The Umayyads rule from Damascus. In Khurasan, black banners rise.
paragraphs: For nearly ninety years the Umayyad family had ruled the caliphate from Damascus, and plenty of Muslims loathed them. From 747 a shadowy organiser called Abu Muslim raised black banners in Khurasan, in eastern Iran, for “a chosen one from the family of the Prophet”. The man chosen was Abu al-Abbas, great-great-grandson of the Prophet's uncle al-Abbas. Late in 749 he was proclaimed caliph in the mosque at Kufa.

Then his army had to win. On 25 January 750, by the Great Zab river in northern Iraq, it routed the last Umayyad caliph, Marwan II. Marwan fled to Egypt and was hunted down and killed that August. The new regime showed no mercy. Umayyad princes were lured to a peace banquet in Palestine and clubbed to death. One young prince, Abd al-Rahman, escaped, reached Spain and made himself ruler of Córdoba in 756.

Abu al-Abbas ruled from Iraq, never from Damascus. In 751 an Abbasid army beat a Chinese Tang force at Talas, deep in Central Asia. But he got only four years. In June 754 smallpox killed him at al-Anbar, aged about 33. His heir was his elder half-brother, Abu Ja'far.

claims.text: The killers ate their dinner on a leather mat spread over the dying Umayyad princes.
claims.note: The massacre at Abu Futrus is widely reported, but the grisly details come from later Arab historians and vary from one telling to the next.

claims.text: The Umayyad tombs were dug up and the corpse of the caliph Hisham flogged and burned.
claims.note: Told by later chroniclers such as al-Mas'udi. Desecration fits the mood of 750, but the story was surely polished in the retelling.

claims.text: “Al-Saffah” means “the shedder of blood”.
claims.note: That is the usual reading, but the word can also mean “the generous”, and it may have been a later label rather than a title he used.

reigns.hook: Al-Saffah is dead after four years. His half-brother Abu Ja'far takes the throne, and the first thing he faces is an uncle who wants it for himself.

reigns.tagline: The penny-pinching killer who built Baghdad
reigns.previously: Smallpox kills al-Saffah. His half-brother Abu Ja'far is the heir.
paragraphs: Abu Ja'far took the name al-Mansur, “the victorious”, and had to earn it fast. His uncle Abd Allah, the victor of the Zab, claimed the throne. Al-Mansur sent Abu Muslim to crush him, then turned on Abu Muslim himself. In 755 the kingmaker of the revolution was summoned to the caliph's camp, berated, and cut down by guards in front of him.

Next came the family of Ali, who felt the revolution had been stolen from them. In 762 Muhammad, “the Pure Soul”, rose at Medina, and his brother Ibrahim rose at Basra. By early 763 both had died in battle. Meanwhile al-Mansur began his masterpiece on the Tigris: Baghdad, officially Madinat al-Salam, the City of Peace. It was a perfect circle of walls with four gates, and his palace and mosque under a green dome at the centre.

He watched every coin, and left a bulging treasury. He also elbowed his nephew Isa ibn Musa out of the succession so that his own son Muhammad would be heir. In October 775 he died on the road to Mecca, on pilgrimage, far from his new city.

claims.text: People nicknamed him “father of farthings” for his stinginess.
claims.note: The nickname, Abu al-Dawaniq, is reported by later Arabic writers. How widely it was used in his lifetime is unknown.

claims.text: After his death a locked storeroom was found full of the labelled corpses of murdered Alids.
claims.note: Told by al-Tabari over a century later. It reads like a moral tale about a ruthless ruler.

claims.text: A hundred graves were dug near Mecca so nobody would know which was his.
claims.note: A later chroniclers' story that fits his reputation for caution; there is no way to check it.

reigns.hook: Al-Mansur is dead on the pilgrim road, and his treasury is bursting. His son al-Mahdi has very different ideas about what money is for.

reigns.tagline: The big spender who opened his father's vaults
reigns.previously: Al-Mansur dies on pilgrimage, leaving a new city and a full treasury.
paragraphs: Al-Mansur died near Mecca, and it took days for the news to reach Baghdad, where his son Muhammad was proclaimed caliph as al-Mahdi. He was everything his father wasn't. He threw open the treasury and handed out gifts and pensions. He also had a hard edge. He hunted down “zindiqs”, heretics, mostly followers of the Manichaean faith, and gave a special inquisitor the job of rooting them out.

In Khurasan a preacher called al-Muqanna, “the Veiled One”, hid his face and drew a big following. He held out for years before dying in his fortress around 780. On the Byzantine frontier, the caliph's young son Harun led a raid in 782 all the way to the Bosporus. The empress Irene, ruling for her boy Constantine VI, agreed to pay a yearly tribute.

At court the real force was al-Mahdi's wife al-Khayzuran, a former slave who now had officials queuing at her door. In August 785 al-Mahdi died on a hunting trip in western Iran. He left two sons by her, Musa and Harun, named heirs in that order.

claims.text: He galloped after a deer into a ruined building and smashed his head on the doorway.
claims.note: One of two versions al-Tabari gives. The other is poison.

claims.text: He ate poisoned food that a jealous slave woman had meant for a rival.
claims.note: Also in al-Tabari, who doesn't choose between the stories. Both may be later gossip.

reigns.hook: Al-Mahdi is dead. His elder son Musa becomes al-Hadi, a hot-tempered young caliph who has no plans to share power with his brother, or with his mother.

reigns.tagline: The hothead who crossed his mother
reigns.previously: Al-Mahdi dies on a hunt. His elder son Musa is next in line.
paragraphs: Musa, now al-Hadi, was away fighting near the Caspian Sea when his father died. His brother Harun kept order and sent him the insignia of office. Al-Hadi hurried back and set about ruling his own way. That meant clipping his mother's wings. Al-Khayzuran was used to generals and officials seeking her favour. Her son told them to stop calling at her door.

He also wanted his own small son Ja'far as heir in place of Harun, and he leaned hard on his brother to give up his rights. Harun's tutor, Yahya the Barmakid, urged him to hold firm and ended up in jail. Then, in September 786, after barely thirteen months on the throne, al-Hadi suddenly died. That same night Harun became caliph.

claims.text: Al-Hadi was smothered by slave girls on his mother's orders.
claims.note: Al-Tabari and others report it among several versions; some blame an illness. Al-Khayzuran certainly had a motive.

claims.text: On the “night of three caliphs” one caliph died, another took the throne and a third was born.
claims.note: The famous tradition: al-Hadi died, Harun succeeded, and Harun's son al-Ma'mun was born. The standard dates fit, but chroniclers loved the neatness.

reigns.hook: One night, three caliphs. The new one is Harun, about twenty years old, with the Barmakid family at his side. Baghdad's golden age is about to begin.

reigns.tagline: The golden-age caliph of the Arabian Nights
reigns.previously: Al-Hadi dies suddenly. His brother Harun takes the throne that night.
paragraphs: Harun took the name al-Rashid, “the rightly guided”, and his reign became the golden age everyone remembers. Baghdad boomed with trade, poets and scholars. For 17 years the real work of government sat with the Barmakids, a family from Balkh: Harun's old tutor Yahya and his sons al-Fadl and Ja'far. Ja'far was the caliph's closest friend.

Then, in January 803, it all fell apart overnight. Ja'far was beheaded, and Yahya, al-Fadl and the rest of the family were jailed. Abroad, Frankish chronicles say Harun sent Charlemagne an elephant called Abul-Abbas, which reached Aachen in 802, and later a water clock. When the Byzantine emperor Nikephoros I stopped paying tribute, Harun marched deep into Anatolia and took Heraclea in 806.

He spent much of his later reign at Raqqa on the Euphrates. In 802 he fixed the succession: al-Amin as heir, then al-Ma'mun, who would hold Khurasan. The pledge was hung in the Ka'ba at Mecca. In 809, marching east to crush a revolt, he fell ill and died at Tus.

claims.text: The Barmakids fell because Ja'far secretly married Harun's sister Abbasa and they had a child.
claims.note: Told by al-Tabari and others as gossip, and loved by later storytellers. Historians suspect the family had simply grown too powerful.

claims.text: Harun answered Nikephoros with a letter addressed to “the Roman dog”.
claims.note: The letter's text is quoted by al-Tabari. It may be genuine, or a later flourish.

claims.text: Harun wandered Baghdad at night in disguise, as in the Thousand and One Nights.
claims.note: The Nights were written down centuries later. Their Harun is a storybook figure, not a historical record.

reigns.hook: Harun dies far from Baghdad. His careful plan splits the empire between two sons, al-Amin in Baghdad and al-Ma'mun in Khurasan. How long can that last?

reigns.tagline: Brother against brother, and Baghdad in ruins
reigns.previously: Harun dies at Tus, leaving the empire split between two sons.
paragraphs: Muhammad al-Amin was the son of Harun and the princess Zubayda, a granddaughter of al-Mansur. He had the perfect pedigree, and Baghdad was his. His half-brother al-Ma'mun held Khurasan from Merv, and Harun's settlement made al-Ma'mun next in line. Al-Amin's advisers wanted that changed. In 810 he named his own son Musa heir. Al-Ma'mun refused to accept it, and the empire slid into civil war.

In 811 al-Ma'mun's general Tahir ibn al-Husayn, with a much smaller army, smashed al-Amin's forces at Rayy. Tahir pushed into Iraq, and by 812 Baghdad was under siege. For a year the city became a battlefield. Catapults wrecked houses, bands of poor street fighters held the barricades for al-Amin, and whole districts burned.

In September 813, with the city lost, al-Amin tried to slip away by boat to surrender to another of his brother's generals. Tahir's men caught him, and he was killed in the night of 24 to 25 September.

claims.text: He was the only Abbasid caliph whose father and mother were both Abbasids.
claims.note: Often repeated by chroniclers and modern historians: Zubayda was al-Mansur's granddaughter, while almost every other caliph had a slave mother.

claims.text: Al-Amin cared more for parties and his eunuch Kawthar than for the war.
claims.note: The sources were written for the winning side under al-Ma'mun, who had every reason to make his brother look unfit.

claims.text: His head was sent to al-Ma'mun in Khurasan.
claims.note: Reported by al-Tabari. Versions of his last night differ in the details.

reigns.hook: Al-Amin is dead and Baghdad is a wreck. The winner, al-Ma'mun, is still far away in Merv, and he's about to make a choice that shocks his own family.

reigns.tagline: The scholar caliph who demanded agreement
reigns.previously: Al-Amin is killed as Baghdad falls. Al-Ma'mun has won the war.
paragraphs: Abd Allah al-Ma'mun was Harun's son by a Persian slave woman, and for years after his victory he stayed in Merv. In 817 he stunned everyone. He named as heir Ali al-Rida, a descendant of the Prophet through Ali, and swapped the Abbasid black for green. Baghdad's Abbasids were furious. They hailed his uncle Ibrahim ibn al-Mahdi, a famous singer, as caliph.

Al-Rida died suddenly at Tus in 818, and al-Ma'mun headed west. He reached Baghdad in 819, Ibrahim's caliphate melted away, and the black came back. Then came the part of his reign people remember. He backed the translation of Greek science and philosophy into Arabic and built observatories in Baghdad and Damascus. The mathematician al-Khwarizmi dedicated his book on algebra to him.

He also wanted the scholars to agree with him. In 833 he began the mihna, an inquisition requiring judges and scholars to declare that the Quran was created. Most gave in. Ahmad ibn Hanbal refused. That August al-Ma'mun died on campaign against Byzantium near Tarsus, naming his brother Abu Ishaq as heir.

claims.text: The House of Wisdom was a great academy of translators and scientists.
claims.note: Later writers made it one. Many historians, such as Dimitri Gutas, see it mainly as a palace library, with the translating paid for by many patrons.

claims.text: Ali al-Rida was poisoned to clear the way back to Baghdad.
claims.note: Shi'a tradition holds that he was poisoned, some say on al-Ma'mun's orders. Other sources record a sudden illness.

claims.text: Aristotle appeared to al-Ma'mun in a dream and inspired the translations.
claims.note: Told by Ibn al-Nadim in his Fihrist, written about 150 years later.

reigns.hook: Al-Ma'mun dies far from home. His brother al-Mu'tasim takes over, bringing a private army of Turkish slave soldiers who will change the caliphate for good.

reigns.tagline: Turkish soldiers, a new capital and a war cry
reigns.previously: Al-Ma'mun dies near Tarsus, naming his brother Abu Ishaq heir.
paragraphs: Abu Ishaq, now al-Mu'tasim, was another of Harun's sons, by a Turkic slave mother. He took the throne ahead of al-Ma'mun's son al-Abbas, thanks to his secret weapon: an army of Turkic slave soldiers, the ghilman, bought in Central Asia and loyal only to him. Baghdad's people hated these swaggering horsemen in their streets. So in 836 he built a new capital, Samarra, about 125 km up the Tigris.

His general al-Afshin finally crushed Babak, whose rebels had held the mountains of Azerbaijan for some twenty years. Babak was taken in 837 and executed at Samarra. That same year the Byzantine emperor Theophilos sacked the frontier town of Zapetra. Al-Mu'tasim hit back in 838 by marching on Amorium, home city of the emperor's family, and took it. The poet Abu Tammam hailed the victory in a famous ode.

Victory bred suspicion. A plot to put al-Abbas on the throne was crushed in 838, and al-Abbas died in prison. In 840 al-Afshin himself was put on trial and died in jail. The mihna went on. Al-Mu'tasim died at Samarra in January 842, and his son Harun succeeded him as al-Wathiq.

claims.text: A captured woman at Zapetra cried “Wa Mu'tasimah!” (“Help, Mu'tasim!”), and he swore to avenge her.
claims.note: A much-loved tale told in later sources. The sack of Amorium is certain; the cry is the stuff of legend.

claims.text: Abu Tammam's ode on Amorium opens: “The sword is truer than books.”
claims.note: The poem survives and is one of the most famous in classical Arabic. The line mocks astrologers who had predicted failure.

claims.text: Ahmad ibn Hanbal was flogged for refusing the mihna's creed.
claims.note: The flogging is well attested, but sources disagree on the year and on how many lashes he took.

reigns.hook: Al-Mu'tasim dies in his new city. His son al-Wathiq inherits Samarra, the inquisition, and a corps of Turkish officers who are learning who really holds the power.

reigns.tagline: The caliph who sent a man to find the end of the world
reigns.reignEnded: Died at Samarra, no heir named
reigns.previously: Al-Mu'tasim dies at Samarra, the city he built for his Turkish army.
paragraphs: Al-Wathiq, whose own name was Harun like his famous grandfather, took over a rich empire run from Samarra. The real muscle now belonged to his father's Turkish commanders. Men like Ashinas and Itakh got grand titles, big estates and the caliph's ear. Al-Wathiq also squeezed the government secretaries, arresting several and stripping them of their fortunes.

Under him the mihna, the test forcing scholars to say the Quran was created, hit its harshest point. In 846 Ahmad ibn Nasr al-Khuza'i, a respected Baghdad scholar accused of plotting a rising, refused to say it and was beheaded. In 845 he had ransomed Muslim captives from Byzantium at the Lamos river. And he sent an interpreter called Sallam east to find the wall Alexander built to hold back Gog and Magog.

He fell ill and died at Samarra in August 847, still in his mid-thirties, without naming an heir. A thousand years later he got a strange afterlife. The English writer William Beckford made him the anti-hero of Vathek, a gothic tale of a cruel, curious caliph who ends up in hell.

claims.text: Al-Wathiq's envoy Sallam travelled to Alexander's wall against Gog and Magog and came back to describe it.
claims.note: Told by the geographer Ibn Khordadbeh, who says he had it from Sallam himself. The route is vague and historians doubt he found any such wall; some think he reached part of the Chinese frontier.

claims.text: Al-Wathiq struck the first blow at Ahmad ibn Nasr's execution with his own sword.
claims.note: Reported by al-Tabari. Ahmad became a martyr to the traditionist scholars, whose later accounts make the scene as dramatic as possible.

claims.text: William Beckford's novel Vathek (1786) is loosely based on al-Wathiq.
claims.note: Beckford wrote it in French and it first came out in English in 1786. He borrowed the caliph's name and some anecdotes, then invented the rest.

reigns.hook: Al-Wathiq is dead and nobody has been named. In a room at Samarra the generals and officials look at his young son, then at his brother Ja'far. They pick the brother. They will live to regret it.

reigns.tagline: The spiral-minaret caliph killed at his own party
reigns.previously: Al-Wathiq dies at Samarra without naming an heir.
paragraphs: Ja'far, who took the name al-Mutawakkil, had been mocked by his brother's court and nobody expected much of him. He soon showed teeth. He had the Turkish commander Itakh arrested, and he ended the mihna, siding with the traditionist scholars like Ahmad ibn Hanbal. He was hard on the Shi'a, and his men levelled the shrine of al-Husayn at Karbala. In 850 he ordered Christians and Jews to wear distinctive dress.

He also loved to build and to spend. At Samarra he raised a huge Great Mosque, finished in 852, with a minaret wound round by a spiral ramp, the Malwiya. It still stands. Then he started a whole new palace-city to the north, al-Ja'fariyya. His court was famous for poets, singers and long nights of wine.

In the end he tried to break the Turkish generals and to push his favourite son al-Mu'tazz ahead of the heir, al-Muntasir. On the night of 10 to 11 December 861 Turkish officers burst into a drinking party at al-Ja'fariyya and cut down the caliph and his friend and minister al-Fath ibn Khaqan.

claims.text: Al-Mutawakkil had the tomb of al-Husayn at Karbala destroyed and the site ploughed and flooded.
claims.note: Al-Tabari records the order. Shi'a and later writers stress it most; how much was actually destroyed, and for how long, is unclear.

claims.text: His son al-Muntasir backed the murder.
claims.note: Widely believed at the time, and he was the one who gained. The chroniclers never prove it, and some say he was dragged along by the plotters.

claims.text: The Great Mosque of Samarra and its spiral minaret were built for al-Mutawakkil between about 848 and 852.
claims.note: Dated by the chroniclers and by archaeology. It was one of the largest mosques in the world, and the minaret is about 52 metres high.

reigns.hook: Al-Mutawakkil lies dead and al-Muntasir is caliph by morning. The soldiers have learnt something dangerous: they can kill a caliph and get away with it.

reigns.cameToPower: Proclaimed the night of the murder
reigns.previously: Turkish officers murder al-Mutawakkil at a drinking party.
paragraphs: Muhammad, called al-Muntasir, was hailed as caliph at Samarra while his father's body was still warm. Everyone knew who gained from the murder, and plenty of people believed he had blessed it. The Turkish commanders who did the killing now stood behind his throne, and he owed them everything.

He moved fast to protect himself. His brothers al-Mu'tazz and al-Mu'ayyad, whom their father had pushed ahead of him, were made to give up their places in the succession. He also eased his father's pressure on the family of Ali. Then, in June 862, after barely six months, he fell ill and died. Rumour said his doctor had bled him with a poisoned lancet, and that the Turks had paid for it.

claims.text: Al-Muntasir backed the plot that killed his father.
claims.note: Widely believed at the time and repeated by al-Tabari's informants. Nothing proves it, and some accounts say the plotters simply used his name.

claims.text: He was killed with a poisoned lancet when his doctor bled him.
claims.note: One of several versions in al-Tabari and al-Mas'udi. Others give a throat illness. Many saw his early death as punishment for his father's murder.

claims.text: He was shaken by a carpet showing a Persian king who killed his father and reigned only six months.
claims.note: A moral tale told by al-Mas'udi and others. It fits his story too neatly to trust.

reigns.hook: Al-Muntasir is dead and his brothers have been cut out of the line. The Turkish chiefs pass them over and pick a quiet cousin, al-Musta'in, who they hope will do as he's told.

reigns.tagline: The caliph the generals picked, then besieged
reigns.previously: Al-Muntasir dies suddenly, six months after his father's murder.
paragraphs: Ahmad, called al-Musta'in, was a grandson of al-Mu'tasim. The Turkish commanders chose him over al-Mutawakkil's sons, who might one day want revenge. He soon learned whose caliph he was. The generals Wasif and Bugha the Younger ran things, and when the soldiers rioted over pay he had nothing to give them.

The empire frayed. In 864 a Shi'a rebel set up his own state in Tabaristan, south of the Caspian. Then the commanders fell out. Early in 865 Wasif and Bugha took al-Musta'in to Baghdad, and the troops left behind at Samarra freed al-Mu'tazz and made him caliph. Baghdad was besieged for most of a year, and the city's people paid in hunger and fire.
Early in 866 al-Musta'in gave in. He abdicated on a promise of safety and was sent off south. The promise did not last the year. In October 866 he was killed by men acting for the new caliph.

claims.text: Al-Musta'in was put to death on al-Mu'tazz's orders despite a promise of safety.
claims.note: Al-Tabari reports the abdication terms and the killing. The details of how he died vary.

claims.text: The Samarra commanders chose him because al-Mutawakkil's sons might avenge their father.
claims.note: A motive the chroniclers suggest. It makes sense, but nobody recorded what the generals actually said.

reigns.hook: Baghdad has surrendered and al-Musta'in is gone. The young al-Mu'tazz is now the only caliph, with an army to pay and an empty treasury.

reigns.tagline: Too young, too broke, and the army wanted paying
reigns.previously: Al-Musta'in abdicates after Baghdad's long siege.
paragraphs: Al-Mu'tazz was al-Mutawakkil's favourite son, the one his father had wanted as heir. Now he had the throne, but he was still a teenager and had no money. He tried to rule by playing the army's factions against each other: the Turks, the Farghanans from Central Asia and the North Africans. His brother al-Mu'ayyad, a possible rival, died in prison in 866.

He lost the two great Turkish chiefs: Wasif was killed by rioting troops in 867, and al-Mu'tazz had Bugha the Younger killed in 868. It did not free him. The provinces stopped sending money, and in 868 a Turkish officer named Ahmad ibn Tulun went to govern Egypt and soon ran it as his own.
In July 869 the troops demanded their pay. He had nothing and asked his mother, Qabiha, who said she had nothing either. The soldiers dragged him from the palace, and within days he was dead.

claims.text: Al-Mu'tazz was beaten, left in the summer heat and shut in a room until he died.
claims.note: Al-Tabari's account. The soldiers announced that he had simply died, and showed the body to witnesses.

claims.text: His mother refused to pay the troops, though a huge hoard of hers was found soon after.
claims.note: Al-Tabari tells it, with large sums. It became a famous tale of greed and may have grown in the telling.

reigns.hook: The soldiers have killed one son of al-Mutawakkil. Now they turn to his nephew al-Muhtadi, a stern, pious man who thinks he can make them behave.

reigns.tagline: The pious caliph who tried to tame the army
reigns.previously: Unpaid troops depose al-Mu'tazz, and he is dead within days.
paragraphs: Muhammad, son of al-Wathiq, took the name al-Muhtadi. He was the opposite of the party caliphs. He sent the singers and the wine away, lived simply and sat in person to hear complaints against officials. He wanted the caliph to be a real ruler again and the generals to obey him.

The timing was bad. In 869 a man named Ali ibn Muhammad raised the slaves who worked the salt marshes near Basra, and the Zanj revolt began. At Samarra the Turkish commanders were split, and al-Muhtadi tried to set them against each other. In 870 he had one of the chiefs, Bayakbak, killed.
Bayakbak's men rose in fury. The caliph's own troops broke, and he was caught. The soldiers deposed him in June 870, and a few days later he was dead.

claims.text: Al-Muhtadi wanted to be to the Abbasids what the pious Umar II had been to the Umayyads.
claims.note: A saying put in his mouth by later writers who admired him. His austere life is well reported.

claims.text: He sat in person to judge complaints against officials.
claims.note: Reported by al-Tabari and al-Mas'udi. These mazalim sessions were part of his effort to restore the caliph's authority.

reigns.hook: The soldiers fetch another son of al-Mutawakkil, al-Mu'tamid, from confinement. He will last 22 years, because his brother is about to do all the real work.

reigns.title: al-Mu'tamid and al-Muwaffaq
reigns.tagline: One brother wore the title, the other ran the war
reigns.previously: The soldiers depose al-Muhtadi, and he is dead within days.
paragraphs: Al-Mu'tamid, whose name was Ahmad, was caliph for 22 years. His younger brother Abu Ahmad, called al-Muwaffaq, was never caliph, but he commanded the army and in practice ran the state. He saved Baghdad in 876 when he beat the Saffarid warlord Ya'qub ibn al-Layth at Dayr al-Aqul. In 882 al-Mu'tamid tried to slip away to Ahmad ibn Tulun in Egypt, but was caught and brought back.

The big fight was the Zanj revolt. Its leader, Ali ibn Muhammad, rallied East African slaves who scraped the salty topsoil off the marshes near Basra, along with peasants and Bedouin. In 871 they sacked Basra. They built their own capital, al-Mukhtara, deep in the marshes. Al-Muwaffaq and his son Abu al-Abbas fought them channel by channel and finally stormed the city in 883. The rebel leader was killed.

Al-Muwaffaq came back worn out by years in the field and died in 891. His son Abu al-Abbas was named heir, pushing aside al-Mu'tamid's own son. When al-Mu'tamid died in October 892 the throne went to his nephew.

claims.text: The Zanj killed hundreds of thousands, and Basra lost most of its people.
claims.note: The medieval chroniclers give enormous figures. Historians treat them as signs of a disaster, not counts.

claims.text: Al-Mu'tamid tried to escape to Ahmad ibn Tulun in Egypt in 882.
claims.note: Al-Tabari tells it. He was stopped on the way by al-Muwaffaq's men and taken back, a caliph in all but freedom.

claims.text: Al-Mu'tamid complained in verse that he could not touch the wealth ruled in his name.
claims.note: Lines attributed to him by later anthologists. They fit his position, but their authorship is uncertain.

reigns.hook: Al-Mu'tamid is dead. His nephew Abu al-Abbas, the hard man who stormed the Zanj capital, takes the throne, and he is moving the court back to Baghdad for good.

reigns.tagline: The tough, thrifty caliph who brought Baghdad back
reigns.previously: Al-Mu'tamid dies after 22 years, a caliph his brother outshone.
paragraphs: Al-Mu'tadid, Ahmad to his family, had learnt to rule in his father's army camps. He made Baghdad the capital again, and Samarra was left to empty out. He was tough and careful with money, and he filled the treasury that the anarchy had emptied. People feared him. The chroniclers tell of grim punishments for rebels and thieves.

He made peace with the Tulunids of Egypt by marrying Qatr al-Nada, the daughter of their ruler Khumarawayh, whose trousseau was the talk of the age. To help farmers he moved the start of the tax year, so the land tax fell due after the harvest. But new trouble was brewing. The Qarmatians, radical Isma'ili rebels, were rising in eastern Arabia and in the Syrian desert. He died in Baghdad in April 902.

claims.text: Qatr al-Nada's trousseau was so vast that it bankrupted Egypt.
claims.note: The chroniclers love the figures, which grew with each telling. The Tulunid treasury did run down, but for many reasons.

claims.text: Al-Mu'tadid used horribly cruel punishments.
claims.note: Al-Mas'udi and others describe them. Writers liked to paint him as a harsh but just ruler, which tends to exaggerate both halves.

claims.text: He moved the start of the tax year so the land tax fell after the harvest.
claims.note: Recorded by several chroniclers. The new date was long remembered as al-Mu'tadid's New Year.

reigns.hook: Al-Mu'tadid is dead and the treasury is full. His son Ali, al-Muktafi, inherits the money, and a desert war against the Qarmatians.

reigns.tagline: A short, sickly reign that won back Egypt
reigns.previously: Al-Mu'tadid dies in Baghdad, leaving a full treasury.
paragraphs: Al-Muktafi, whose name was Ali, started with a war. Qarmatian bands were raiding Syria and had besieged Damascus. In 903 his army crushed them, and their captured leaders were paraded through Baghdad and executed. Then his general Muhammad ibn Sulayman marched on Egypt and in 905 ended the Tulunid dynasty. Egypt was back under Baghdad.

At sea things went the other way. In 904 Leo of Tripoli, a Greek convert to Islam who led an Arab fleet, sacked Thessalonica, the Byzantine empire's second city, and carried off thousands of captives. Al-Muktafi was often ill, and he died in August 908 in his early thirties. His officials chose his brother Ja'far, a boy of 12, perhaps because a boy would be easy to steer.

claims.text: Leo of Tripoli sacked Thessalonica in 904 and took thousands of captives.
claims.note: Described by John Kaminiates, a Thessalonian who was taken captive, and confirmed by Arab writers.

claims.text: The officials chose the boy Ja'far because they thought he would be easy to control.
claims.note: That is how the chroniclers explain it. It may be hindsight from the disasters of his reign.

claims.text: Al-Muktafi left a treasury even fuller than his father's.
claims.note: The chroniclers give big figures for the gold left in Baghdad. They were writing after al-Muqtadir had spent it all.

reigns.hook: A 12-year-old is caliph. Within months a group of courtiers decides to replace him with a famous poet.

reigns.tagline: The boy caliph of silver trees and empty coffers
reigns.previously: Al-Muktafi dies young, and the officials pick a boy as caliph.
paragraphs: Ja'far, called al-Muqtadir, was the first boy caliph. In December 908 a court party crowned the poet Ibn al-Mu'tazz instead. He lasted a day, then was caught and put to death. After that the boy reigned for 24 years while viziers like Ibn al-Furat and the honest Ali ibn Isa rose and fell. His mother Shaghab ran the palace, and one of her women, Thamal, even sat as a judge.

Baghdad still dazzled. Byzantine envoys came in 917 and were shown a tree of silver with mechanical singing birds. In 921 Ibn Fadlan set out on a mission to the Volga Bulgars and saw a Rus chief burned in his ship. At home the mystic al-Hallaj, who had cried "I am the Truth", was executed in 922. In 930 the Qarmatians sacked Mecca and carried off the Black Stone.

The money ran out and the army turned on him. In 929 he was deposed for two days, then restored. In 932 his top commander Mu'nis marched on Baghdad. Al-Muqtadir rode out to fight and was killed by Mu'nis's troops outside the city.

claims.text: Byzantine ambassadors in 917 saw a silver tree whose mechanical birds sang.
claims.note: Described by later Baghdad writers, especially al-Khatib al-Baghdadi. The embassy is real; the details may have grown.

claims.text: Ibn Fadlan watched a Rus ship funeral on the Volga.
claims.note: His own eyewitness account survives. It is one of the most vivid and most disturbing descriptions of the Rus.

claims.text: A stewardess called Thamal sat in judgement in a court of appeal.
claims.note: Reported by the chroniclers as a scandal, which suggests it happened, but they were keen to blame women for the reign's failures.

reigns.hook: Al-Muqtadir's body lies outside Baghdad. The generals put his brother al-Qahir on the throne, a man with a temper and no money.

reigns.tagline: Broke, brutal, and blinded within eighteen months
reigns.previously: Al-Muqtadir dies fighting his own general's troops outside Baghdad.
paragraphs: Muhammad, a son of al-Mu'tadid, took the name al-Qahir, "the Conqueror". Mu'nis, the commander whose troops had just killed al-Muqtadir, put him on the throne. The treasury was empty and al-Qahir wanted money. He turned on his brother's family and had their mother Shaghab tortured to find where she had hidden her wealth. She died soon after.

He did not stay grateful to his kingmakers. In 933 he had Mu'nis and his allies killed. By then nobody trusted him. In April 934 his officers broke into the palace and seized him. He refused to abdicate, so they blinded him, which made him unfit to rule.
He lived for another sixteen years or so, poor and forgotten in Baghdad.

claims.text: Al-Qahir had al-Muqtadir's mother tortured for her money.
claims.note: Reported by Miskawayh and other chroniclers. How much she still had, and what they found, is less clear.

claims.text: The blind al-Qahir ended up begging in a mosque.
claims.note: A story told by later historians as a moral lesson. Others say he was kept in the palace on a pension.

reigns.hook: Al-Qahir is blind and out. The officers bring a son of al-Muqtadir, al-Radi, from the prison where al-Qahir had locked him up.

reigns.tagline: The caliph who signed his own power away
reigns.cameToPower: Freed from prison by the officers
reigns.previously: Al-Qahir's officers depose him and blind him.
paragraphs: Muhammad, called al-Radi, was a son of al-Muqtadir and a cultivated young man who wrote poetry. His tutor was the scholar and chess master al-Suli. The money problem had not gone away. His vizier Ibn Muqla, one of the most famous calligraphers in Islamic history, could not fix it, and the provinces kept their taxes.

In 936 al-Radi gave up. He made Ibn Ra'iq, governor of Wasit and Basra, amir al-umara, "commander of commanders", and handed him the army, the taxes and the government. The caliph kept his title, his name on the coins and in the Friday prayer, and not much else. Ibn Muqla schemed to get back in and had his right hand cut off.
Ibn Ra'iq was soon pushed out by the Turkish general Bajkam. Al-Radi died of illness in December 940, about 31 years old.

claims.text: In 936 al-Radi handed real power to Ibn Ra'iq as amir al-umara.
claims.note: Recorded by Miskawayh and later chroniclers. It is usually treated as the moment the caliphs stopped governing.

claims.text: Al-Radi was the last caliph to preach the Friday sermon himself and keep the old court ways.
claims.note: Al-Suli and later writers listed things he was the last to do. A neat story, but he had already lost real power in 936.

reigns.hook: Al-Radi is dead. The general Bajkam lets the officials choose his brother Ibrahim, who becomes al-Muttaqi, the pious one. He will need more than piety.

reigns.tagline: He trusted a general's oath and lost his eyes
reigns.cameToPower: Chosen with the general Bajkam's consent
reigns.previously: Al-Radi dies of illness, a caliph with a title and little else.
paragraphs: Ibrahim, another son of al-Muqtadir, became al-Muttaqi. Within months the general Bajkam was killed on a hunting trip, and Baghdad turned into a prize. Turkish officers, Ibn Ra'iq again, and the Baridi brothers of Basra all fought for it. Each one wanted the caliph in his pocket.

In 942 al-Muttaqi fled north to the Hamdanids of Mosul. They brought him back and their chief, Nasir al-Dawla, took the post of amir al-umara. Then the Turkish general Tuzun drove them out. The caliph fled again, to Raqqa on the Euphrates. The ruler of Egypt, al-Ikhshid, came to meet him there and offered him a safe home in Egypt.
Al-Muttaqi chose to go home. Tuzun swore he would be safe. In October 944, near Baghdad, Tuzun's men seized him and blinded him. He lived on in confinement for more than twenty years.

claims.text: Al-Muttaqi turned down al-Ikhshid's offer of refuge in Egypt and trusted Tuzun's oath.
claims.note: Told by Miskawayh and the later chroniclers. The meeting at Raqqa in 944 is well recorded.

claims.text: Tuzun swore solemn oaths on the Quran for the caliph's safety before blinding him.
claims.note: The chroniclers stress the broken oaths to blacken Tuzun. The betrayal is certain; the exact oaths may be dressed up.

reigns.hook: Tuzun has a blind ex-caliph and needs a new one. He picks al-Mustakfi, a son of al-Muktafi. Out in western Iran, a family of mountain soldiers called the Buyids is watching.

reigns.tagline: Caliph when the Buyids marched in, blind soon after
reigns.previously: Tuzun blinds al-Muttaqi and wants a new caliph.
paragraphs: Abdallah, a son of the caliph al-Muktafi, took the name al-Mustakfi. He was Tuzun's man. When Tuzun died in 945 there was nobody strong left in Baghdad. Hunger and disorder gripped the city.

In December 945 the Buyids arrived. They were three brothers from Daylam, the rainy mountains south of the Caspian, and they were Shi'a. The youngest, Ahmad, marched into Baghdad, and the caliph gave him the title Mu'izz al-Dawla, "Strengthener of the State".

The partnership lasted weeks. In January 946 Mu'izz al-Dawla came to the palace with his men. They pulled al-Mustakfi from his throne, dragged him off, and blinded him. He died in prison a few years later.

claims.text: For a while three blind ex-caliphs were alive in Baghdad at once.
claims.note: Al-Qahir, al-Muttaqi and al-Mustakfi were all still alive in 946, according to the chroniclers' dates. Blinding made a man unfit to rule without killing him.

claims.text: Mu'izz al-Dawla deposed al-Mustakfi because he suspected him of plotting against the Buyids.
claims.note: The reason Miskawayh and later writers give. The Buyids also simply wanted a caliph they had chosen themselves.

reigns.hook: The Buyids hold Baghdad. They are Shi'a, but Mu'izz al-Dawla puts a Sunni caliph, al-Muti, on the throne. A caliph who signs what he's told is worth more to them than a revolution.

reigns.previously: Mu'izz al-Dawla has al-Mustakfi dragged off his throne and blinded.
paragraphs: Al-Fadl, another son of al-Muqtadir, was picked by Mu'izz al-Dawla and took the name al-Muti li-llah, "Obedient to God". Obedience to the amir was what the job really asked. The Buyid amir gave him an allowance and kept the government. The caliph's name stayed on the coins and in the Friday prayer, as far away as Bukhara, and he lost almost everything else.

The Buyids still needed him. Only a caliph could hand out the grand titles they wore, ending in al-Dawla, "of the State". In 963 Baghdad saw public Shi'a mourning for al-Husayn on Ashura, the tenth of Muharram, and Sunni Baghdad did not like it. In 969 the rival Fatimid caliphs, Shi'a Isma'ilis, took Egypt and began building Cairo.

Mu'izz al-Dawla died in 967 and his son Izz al-Dawla was weaker. In 974 the Turkish troops rose under their commander Sebüktegin. Al-Muti, partly paralysed by a stroke, was made to abdicate in August for his son, and he died weeks later.

claims.text: Public Shi'a mourning for Ashura was first held in Baghdad in 963 under Mu'izz al-Dawla.
claims.note: The chroniclers date it to 352 AH (963). Some historians think smaller observances came earlier; this was the first official one.

claims.text: Mu'izz al-Dawla thought about making a descendant of Ali caliph, but was warned he could not control one.
claims.note: Told by later chroniclers such as Ibn al-Athir. It reads like a tidy explanation written with hindsight.

reigns.hook: Al-Muti has stepped down and his son al-Ta'i takes the throne, raised by rebel Turkish troops. Soon the greatest of the Buyids will come to Baghdad, and he wants to be called King of Kings.

reigns.tagline: Married to the amir's daughter, dragged off by his robe
reigns.cameToPower: Raised up during a Turkish revolt
reigns.reignEnded: Pulled off his throne by the Buyids
reigns.previously: A stroke leaves al-Muti paralysed, and he steps down for his son.
paragraphs: Abd al-Karim took the throne as al-Ta'i in 974, in the middle of a mutiny. The Turkish general Sebüktegin had turned on the Buyid amir of Baghdad, and the rebels wanted a caliph of their own making. So the old, sick al-Muti stepped aside and his son was raised up. The Buyids soon got Baghdad back, and the new caliph learned what his father had known: the title was his, the power was theirs.

In 977 the greatest of the Buyids, 'Adud al-Dawla, took Baghdad. He called himself shahanshah, King of Kings, received grand robes and titles from the caliph in a lavish ceremony, and married a daughter to him. When 'Adud al-Dawla died in 983, his sons fought over his empire, and the caliph was a prize to be held.

In 991 the amir Baha al-Dawla was short of cash. He came to an audience at the palace, and his men pulled al-Ta'i off his throne and plundered his treasure. A cousin was fetched to replace him. Al-Ta'i lived on in the palace, a prisoner, until about 1003.

claims.text: 'Adud al-Dawla married his daughter to al-Ta'i hoping for a grandson on the caliph's throne.
claims.note: The marriage is in the chronicles; the motive is the historians' guess, and no such heir ever reigned.

claims.text: Baha al-Dawla's men hauled al-Ta'i off his throne by his robe.
claims.note: A vivid detail from the Baghdad chroniclers; the deposition and the looting are certain, the exact scene may be polished.

claims.text: The new caliph treated his deposed cousin kindly and kept him in comfort.
claims.note: Reported by later chroniclers; little is known of al-Ta'i's last twelve years.

reigns.hook: The new caliph, al-Qadir, is a grandson of al-Muqtadir with no army at all. He is about to reign for forty years and outlast the men who chose him.

reigns.tagline: The patient caliph who outlasted his masters
reigns.previously: The Buyid amir pulls al-Ta'i off his throne and wants a new caliph.
paragraphs: Ahmad, grandson of the caliph al-Muqtadir, was 44 when the Buyids gave him the throne as al-Qadir. They wanted a puppet. They got a slow, stubborn survivor. He had no army, so he used the one weapon a caliph still held: the right to say what Sunni Islam was.

In 1011 he issued the Baghdad Manifesto. Scholars and notables signed a statement that the Fatimid caliphs of Cairo were not descended from the Prophet's daughter Fatima at all. Later he put out a statement of Sunni belief, the Qadiri creed, to be read to the faithful. Far to the east, Mahmud of Ghazni, the Turkish conqueror who raided deep into India, sent his loyalty to Baghdad, took grand titles from the caliph and sent gifts.
The Buyids, meanwhile, split and quarrelled. Al-Qadir reigned 40 years and died in 1031, an old man, with his son already named as heir.

claims.text: The Baghdad Manifesto of 1011 declared the Fatimids' family tree a fake.
claims.note: Reported by several Baghdad chroniclers, who give the names of the signatories.

claims.text: Al-Qadir proclaimed a written creed of Sunni belief.
claims.note: The text survives only in later sources, and historians argue over when it was issued and what it first said.

claims.text: Mahmud of Ghazni sent the caliph rich spoils from his Indian raids.
claims.note: Mahmud's loyalty and titles are certain; the details of the gifts come from court chroniclers keen to flatter him.

reigns.hook: His son al-Qa'im takes the throne. Out on the steppe, a Turkish clan called the Seljuks is on the move, and they will want what only a caliph can give.

reigns.tagline: He crowned a sultan, then lost Baghdad to a rebel
reigns.previously: Al-Qadir dies after 40 years, and his son is ready.
paragraphs: Al-Qa'im inherited a capital run by soldiers. The Turkish commander al-Basasiri held the real power in Baghdad, while out east the Seljuk Turks swept across Iran. In 1055 their leader, Tughril Beg, rode into Baghdad. The caliph named him sultan, "holder of power". The Buyids were finished, and a Sunni strongman now did the ruling.

Then it went wrong. In 1058, while Tughril was away, al-Basasiri seized Baghdad and had the Friday prayer said for the Fatimid caliph of Cairo. Al-Qa'im was packed off into exile on the Euphrates for a year. Tughril came back in 1059, put the caliph back on his throne, and al-Basasiri was hunted down and killed.

The rescue had a price. Tughril pushed the caliph to give him a daughter as a wife. Under his nephew Alp Arslan the Seljuks crushed the Byzantines at Manzikert in 1071, and their vizier Nizam al-Mulk opened his great Nizamiyya college in Baghdad. Al-Qa'im died in 1075, after 44 years.

claims.text: In exile the caliph was held at Haditha on the Euphrates.
claims.note: Most chroniclers say Haditha; some say the nearby town of Ana.

claims.text: Al-Basasiri sent the caliph's robe and insignia to Cairo as trophies.
claims.note: Reported in the chronicles; the details vary between versions.

claims.text: Tughril forced the caliph to marry him his daughter, then died before the marriage could really begin.
claims.note: The wedding (1062) and Tughril's death (1063) are certain; the chroniclers tell the bargaining in different ways.

reigns.hook: Al-Qa'im's son died before him, so the throne goes to a grandson of about 19, al-Muqtadi. The Seljuk sultans are at the height of their power, and they mean to keep the caliph in his place.

reigns.tagline: The caliph a sultan tried to throw out of Baghdad
reigns.previously: Al-Qa'im dies after 44 years. His grandson takes the throne.
paragraphs: Abd Allah was about 19 when he succeeded his grandfather as al-Muqtadi. His father had died young, so the old caliph had kept the boy close as his heir. The real master of the age was the Seljuk sultan Malik-Shah, whose vizier, Nizam al-Mulk, ran an empire stretching from Central Asia to Syria. The caliph's name stayed on the coins and in the Friday prayer, and every sultan still wanted his blessing.

The two families were tied by marriage: al-Muqtadi wed Malik-Shah's daughter in a famously grand wedding. It went badly, and she went home to her father. In 1092 things turned ugly. Nizam al-Mulk was stabbed to death by an assassin dressed as a Sufi, and Malik-Shah ordered the caliph to leave Baghdad. Within weeks the sultan himself was dead.
Malik-Shah's sons and widow fought over his empire. In the middle of the scramble, in February 1094, al-Muqtadi died suddenly, still under 40.

claims.text: Malik-Shah ordered the caliph out of Baghdad and died before it could happen.
claims.note: Told by Ibn al-Athir and other chroniclers, who saw the sultan's sudden death as a judgement; the order itself is hard to pin down.

claims.text: The Seljuk princess left al-Muqtadi because he neglected her.
claims.note: The marriage is certain; the chroniclers' reasons for its failure read like court gossip.

claims.text: Al-Muqtadi was poisoned.
claims.note: A rumour about a sudden death in a dangerous year; no chronicler could prove it.

reigns.hook: His teenage son al-Mustazhir takes the throne. The Seljuk princes are at each other's throats, and far to the west an army of Franks is about to set out for Jerusalem.

reigns.tagline: A bookish caliph while the crusaders took Jerusalem
reigns.previously: Al-Muqtadi dies suddenly as Malik-Shah's sons fight over his empire.
paragraphs: Ahmad was about 16 when he became al-Mustazhir. Outside the palace the Seljuk princes Berkyaruq and Muhammad fought each other for more than ten years, and Baghdad changed hands with their fortunes. The caliph kept his head down. He was a mild, bookish man, and he gave East Baghdad a new wall.

The great scholar al-Ghazali, then teaching at the Nizamiyya college, wrote an attack on the Isma'ilis, the sect behind the Assassins, and named it after him: the Mustazhiri. Then, in July 1099, the First Crusade took Jerusalem. Refugees reached Baghdad and begged for help. Nobody came.
In 1111 angry Syrians broke up Friday prayers in Baghdad and smashed a pulpit to demand a holy war. Al-Mustazhir was annoyed that it spoiled his wedding to the sultan's sister. He died in 1118.

claims.text: Refugees from Jerusalem wept in Baghdad's great mosque, and nobody sent an army.
claims.note: Ibn al-Athir tells the scene, writing over a century later; the lack of any rescue is certain.

claims.text: In 1111 protesters smashed the pulpit of a Baghdad mosque to demand war on the Franks.
claims.note: Reported by the Damascus chronicler Ibn al-Qalanisi, who lived through it, and by later writers.

claims.text: Al-Ghazali wrote the Mustazhiri at the caliph's request.
claims.note: Al-Ghazali says so himself in the book and in his autobiography, The Deliverer from Error.

reigns.hook: His son al-Mustarshid is 26 and restless. He has watched sultans push his family around for long enough, and he means to raise an army of his own.

reigns.tagline: The caliph who rode out to fight the sultans
reigns.reignEnded: Killed by Assassins in his tent
reigns.previously: Al-Mustazhir dies in 1118, a quiet caliph to the end.
paragraphs: Al-Fadl, who took the name al-Mustarshid, was done with sitting still. He built up his own troops and led them himself. In 1123 he beat Dubays, the Arab lord of Hilla, in battle. When the Seljuk sultan Mahmud marched on Baghdad in 1126, the caliph fought back before making peace. In 1133 he even laid siege to Mosul, held by its tough Turkish governor Zengi, though he had to give up.

In 1135 he went for the biggest prize and took the field against Sultan Mas'ud. Near Hamadan his Turkish troops deserted him, and the caliph of Islam was taken prisoner. Mas'ud kept him in his camp. Near Maragha, a band of Assassins slipped into the caliph's tent on 29 August and killed him.
Many people believed the sultan had let it happen. Nobody could prove it.

claims.text: Al-Mustarshid was murdered by Assassins, and Sultan Mas'ud let it happen.
claims.note: The murder is confirmed by every chronicle; the sultan's part rests on suspicion, and Ibn al-Athir reports it as rumour.

claims.text: The caliph's own Turkish soldiers changed sides in the battle near Hamadan.
claims.note: Ibn al-Athir and other chroniclers agree that desertions decided the battle.

reigns.hook: In Baghdad his son al-Rashid is proclaimed caliph. He is furious, and Sultan Mas'ud is about to send him a bill.

reigns.cameToPower: Heir proclaimed on his father's murder
reigns.previously: Assassins murder al-Mustarshid in the sultan's camp near Maragha.
paragraphs: Mansur, called al-Rashid, took the throne in grief and anger. Sultan Mas'ud wanted money and obedience from Baghdad. The new caliph refused both. He gathered allies among the sultan's enemies, among them Zengi of Mosul, and got ready to fight.

In 1136 Mas'ud came to Baghdad with his army. Al-Rashid's allies melted away and he fled north to Mosul. The sultan then did something new: he had judges and lawyers meet and rule the caliph unfit, and in August 1136 they declared him deposed.
Al-Rashid wandered from court to court looking for support. In June 1138, near Isfahan, Assassins killed him, just as they had killed his father.

claims.text: Mas'ud had al-Rashid deposed by a formal hearing of judges and scholars.
claims.note: Ibn al-Athir and other chroniclers describe the hearing; what the witnesses said against him is less certain.

claims.text: Mas'ud wanted the caliph to pay a huge sum demanded from his father.
claims.note: The quarrel over money is in the chronicles; the sums given vary.

reigns.hook: Mas'ud picks al-Rashid's uncle, al-Muqtafi, as caliph, expecting a quiet puppet. He has misjudged him. The Seljuk empire is cracking, and the caliph means to slip through the gap.

reigns.tagline: The puppet who cut his own strings
reigns.previously: Sultan Mas'ud has al-Rashid deposed and wants a quieter caliph.
paragraphs: Muhammad, son of al-Mustazhir, was 40 when Sultan Mas'ud made him caliph as al-Muqtafi. He looked like a safe choice. For 16 years he behaved like one, saying little while the sultan's men ran Baghdad.

Mas'ud died in 1152, and the Seljuk princes went back to fighting each other. Al-Muqtafi moved fast. He threw the sultan's officials out, built an army, and with his clever vizier Ibn Hubayra took control of Iraq. In 1157 the sultan Muhammad came to besiege Baghdad. The walls held, the sultan's troops lost heart, and he went home.
For the first time in two centuries, a caliph ruled his own capital and the land around it. Al-Muqtafi died in 1160, the master of Iraq.

claims.text: The sultan Muhammad's siege of Baghdad in 1157 failed.
claims.note: Reported by Ibn al-Athir and other chroniclers; the sultan withdrew without taking the city.

claims.text: Mas'ud chose al-Muqtafi because he seemed the least likely to cause trouble.
claims.note: This is how the chroniclers explain the choice, with hindsight; the sultan's real reasons are not recorded.

reigns.hook: His son al-Mustanjid inherits a real state with a real army. Keeping it will mean taming the ambitious men around his own throne.

reigns.tagline: Strong at home, killed in his own bathhouse
reigns.reignEnded: Died in a bathhouse, probably murdered
reigns.previously: Al-Muqtafi dies in 1160, master of Iraq after two centuries.
paragraphs: Yusuf, al-Mustanjid, had to fight for his inheritance before it began. As his father lay dying, a rival in the harem wanted her own son on the throne. Al-Mustanjid kept Ibn Hubayra as his vizier and held on to Iraq. The chroniclers say he cut unfair taxes and came down hard on corrupt officials.

Far to the west, the Syrian ruler Nur al-Din was fighting the crusaders and eyeing Egypt, where the Fatimid caliphs were failing. In 1169 Nur al-Din's man, a Kurdish officer called Saladin, became vizier in Cairo.
At home the caliph made dangerous enemies among his own commanders and officials. In December 1170 he fell ill and was taken to the bathhouse. He never came out alive.

claims.text: Courtiers shut al-Mustanjid in a hot bathhouse and left him to die.
claims.note: The chroniclers blame court plotters; it could not be proved, and some accounts say he was simply ill.

claims.text: A woman of the harem armed slave girls with knives to kill him on his father's deathbed, so her son could reign.
claims.note: A dramatic story told by Ibn al-Athir; the details cannot be checked.

claims.text: He abolished unfair taxes and punished corrupt officials.
claims.note: Praised by the chroniclers; how far it went in practice is not known.

reigns.hook: The plotters put his son al-Mustadi on the throne. Within months, great news is coming from Cairo.

reigns.cameToPower: Raised up by his father's killers
reigns.previously: Al-Mustanjid dies in a bathhouse, probably killed by his own court.
paragraphs: Al-Hasan took the throne as al-Mustadi, put there by the court faction that had seen off his father. He was generous and easy-going, and the strongmen around him did much of the ruling at first.

Then, in September 1171, came news from Egypt. On the orders of Nur al-Din, Saladin had the Friday prayer in Cairo read in al-Mustadi's name. The Fatimid caliph al-Adid was dying, and he died days later. After more than 260 years the rival Shi'a caliphate was gone, and the whole Sunni world named one caliph again.
Baghdad was lively. Crowds packed in to hear the fiery preacher Ibn al-Jawzi, a favourite of the caliph. Al-Mustadi died in 1180, leaving a strong caliphate to his son.

claims.text: Saladin's switch of the Friday prayer to al-Mustadi ended the Fatimid caliphate.
claims.note: Reported by Ibn al-Athir and the Egyptian chroniclers; al-Adid was the last Fatimid caliph.

claims.text: Al-Adid died without ever being told he had been dropped from the prayer.
claims.note: Ibn al-Athir says his family kept it from him; other writers do not mention it.

claims.text: Ibn al-Jawzi drew crowds of tens of thousands to his sermons.
claims.note: The numbers come from Ibn al-Jawzi himself and his admirers, who were not shy about his fame.

reigns.hook: The new caliph, al-Nasir, is 21, clever and very ambitious. He wants more than Iraq. He wants to be the centre of the whole Islamic world again.

reigns.tagline: The caliph who played kingmaker for 46 years
reigns.previously: Al-Mustadi dies, leaving a caliphate with real power again.
paragraphs: Al-Nasir reigned longer than any other Abbasid caliph, and he used every year. He played the great powers against each other. He backed the Khwarazmshah Tekish against the last Great Seljuk sultan, Tughril III, who was killed in battle in 1194. The Seljuks who had bossed the caliphs for nearly 140 years were gone.

He also made the caliph cool again. He joined the futuwwa, the brotherhoods of young men with their own codes of honour, and made himself their head. He ran pigeon-racing and crossbow clubs too. Then Tekish's son, Muhammad II, turned on him and marched on Baghdad in 1217. Snow in the Zagros mountains wrecked his army before it got there.
In 1221 al-Nasir built the Talisman Gate in Baghdad's walls. He died in 1225, old and ill, leaving a strong, rich caliphate. Out east, the Mongols had already arrived.

claims.text: Al-Nasir invited the Mongols to attack the Khwarazmshah.
claims.note: Made by later writers hostile to him; there is no solid evidence, though he certainly wanted Muhammad II beaten.

claims.text: He went blind in one eye in his last years.
claims.note: Reported by chroniclers writing about his final illness; details vary.

claims.text: The Talisman Gate stood until the Ottomans blew it up in 1917.
claims.note: The retreating Ottoman army used it as a powder store and blew it up as the British took Baghdad.

reigns.tagline: Nine kind months after a long wait
reigns.previously: Al-Nasir dies after nearly 46 years, leaving a rich caliphate.
paragraphs: Muhammad, al-Zahir, had waited most of his life. His father named him heir long before, then turned cold and favoured a younger son. Only after that brother died was al-Zahir's place safe. He came to the throne in 1225, nearly 50 years old.

He set out to undo his father's harshness. He opened the prisons, gave back property al-Nasir had seized, and cut taxes and fines. When officials warned him he was emptying the treasury, he is said to have answered that he had opened his shop late in the day, so let him do some good while he could.
He had nine months. Al-Zahir died in July 1226, and Baghdad mourned him.

claims.text: Al-Zahir freed prisoners, returned seized property and cut taxes.
claims.note: The chroniclers praise him warmly, but nine months is too short to test a reputation.

claims.text: He said he had opened his shop late, so he must do good quickly.
claims.note: A famous saying in Ibn al-Athir's chronicle; it sounds polished, as good stories do.

reigns.hook: His son al-Mustansir takes the throne. He has money, peace and big plans for Baghdad, and he is going to build.

reigns.tagline: He built Baghdad's grandest college
reigns.previously: Al-Zahir dies after nine gentle months on the throne.
paragraphs: Mansur, al-Mustansir, built the Mustansiriya, a huge college on the Tigris that opened in the early 1230s. It taught all four schools of Sunni law under one roof, with a great library, a kitchen and baths for students. The building still stands in Baghdad.
These were rich, confident years. In 1237 the artist Yahya al-Wasiti painted the Maqamat of al-Hariri in Baghdad, full of camels, markets, mosques and sharp-tongued tricksters.
But the Mongols were coming closer. Their raiding parties reached Iraq in the 1230s, and al-Mustansir had to spend on soldiers as well as scholars. He died in December 1242.

claims.text: The Mustansiriya had a famous water clock that told the hours.
claims.note: Described by chroniclers; nothing of it survives.

claims.text: The Mustansiriya's building still stands in Baghdad.
claims.note: Much restored, but the original 13th-century college survives on the bank of the Tigris.

claims.text: Al-Mustansir built up a large army to face the Mongols.
claims.note: The chroniclers say he raised troops; the numbers they give are not reliable.

reigns.hook: Al-Mustansir's son al-Musta'sim takes the throne. He has a rich capital, a quarrelling court and a small army. And far to the east, the Mongol empire is still growing.

reigns.tagline: The last caliph of Baghdad
reigns.previously: Al-Mustansir dies. Mongol raiders already prowl the borders.
paragraphs: Al-Musta'sim was the 37th Abbasid caliph, and the last to rule from Baghdad. The chroniclers paint him as gentle, fond of pigeons and music, and not up to the job. His court was split between the Shi'a vizier Ibn al-Alqami and the commander Aybeg, the Dawatdar. Meanwhile the Great Khan Möngke sent his brother Hulagu west. In 1256 the Assassins' mountain castles fell. Baghdad was next.

Hulagu demanded submission. The caliph refused. In January 1258 his army was beaten when the Mongols broke the Tigris dykes and flooded its camp. The siege began on 29 January, and on 10 February Baghdad surrendered. For about a week the Mongols killed and looted. Medieval chroniclers give death tolls from 200,000 to 800,000 or more; nobody knows the true number.
On 20 February al-Musta'sim was executed. Five centuries of the Abbasids in Baghdad were over. A relative was later set up as caliph in Cairo, a figurehead for the Mamluk sultans.

claims.text: The caliph was rolled in a carpet and trampled by horses, so no royal blood touched the ground.
claims.note: A tradition in several Persian and Arabic histories, fitting a Mongol taboo on royal blood. Marco Polo's legend has him starved among his gold in a tower.

claims.text: So many books were thrown into the Tigris that it ran black with ink.
claims.note: A famous image from later writers; libraries were surely looted, but the detail cannot be checked.

claims.text: The vizier Ibn al-Alqami betrayed Baghdad to the Mongols.
claims.note: Sunni writers accused him; the evidence is thin and the charge was coloured by sectarian feeling.
